title: Aphasia Sorter
description: A classification game in which students read short original speech samples, each with a one-line clue about comprehension or repetition, and sort them as Broca's aphasia, Wernicke's aphasia, conduction aphasia, or normal speech. Immediate feedback explains which clue decides each answer, and a running score tracks progress over 10 shuffled items.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: Neuroscience
learningObjectives: Classify short speech samples as Broca's aphasia, Wernicke's aphasia, conduction aphasia, or normal speech by analyzing fluency, comprehension, and repetition, scoring at least 8 of 10 correct.
Explain which clue (fluency, comprehension, or repetition) distinguishes each type of aphasia.
prerequisites: Each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body (Chapter 4)
Definitions of fluency, telegraphic speech, paraphasia, neologism, comprehension, and repetition (Chapter 12, Section 12.4)
keyQuestions: Is the speech fluent or nonfluent?
Does the person understand what is said to them?
Can the person repeat a sentence word for word?
Why can fluent speech still be a sign of a serious language disorder?
misconceptions: Fluent speech means language is normal.
People with Broca's aphasia cannot understand language.
Pauses and filler words like 'um' always signal aphasia.
Aphasia means a loss of intelligence.
controls: Broca's button: classify the current sample as Broca's aphasia
Wernicke's button: classify the current sample as Wernicke's aphasia
Conduction button: classify the current sample as conduction aphasia
Normal button: classify the current sample as normal speech
Next button: go to the next sample after answering
Restart button: reshuffle the 10 items and reset the score

simulationModel.items: 10 original speech samples: 3 Broca's, 3 Wernicke's, 2 conduction, 2 normal
simulationModel.scoring: One attempt per item; score = number correct out of number answered; mastery at 8 of 10
simulationModel.assumptions: Speech samples are simplified, original teaching examples that show textbook-typical patterns.
simulationModel.limitations: Real aphasia varies widely and often mixes features; global, anomic, transcortical, and primary progressive aphasia are not included; samples are text only, so speech rhythm and effort are described rather than heard.

accessibility: Text wraps to the container width; minimum text size 14 px; native HTML buttons support keyboard focus; screen-reader description via p5.js describe().
